description:
Bracken Team is a group of passionate developers and problem-solvers from Irbid, Jordan, with experience in software development, AI/ML, rapid prototyping, and hackathons.

We are proud to have one of the members of the winning team of 2025 NASA Space Apps Challenge Irbid.
summary:
CAIRN (Crew Assisted Integrated Route Navigator) is a web app that plans and simulates walks for the first astronauts on Mars. It uses official NASA, USGS and JPL data at three real sites: Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and Deuteronilus Mensae.

On Mars, a message to Earth takes 3 to 22 minutes each way, so when something goes wrong outside, the crew must decide alone. CAIRN gives them the answers before they leave the rover. It finds the safest walking route over 1-metre HiRISE terrain. It budgets oxygen, time and radiation, checks they can always walk back with a reserve, keeps a shelter within 30 minutes, and maps radio contact and relay masts.

It replays the real 20 May 2024 solar storm and reroutes the crew to safety. Mission Control on Earth sees everything one light time late. In free roam, anyone can walk the terrain with real Mars-gravity physics, alone or with a second astronaut.

CAIRN turns the challenge’s Martian map into a survival guide: every number traces to a real source, and every assumption is labelled.
details:
What it does and how it works

CAIRN (Crew Assisted Integrated Route Navigator) plans and simulates EVAs, walks on foot outside a pressurised rover, for the first crews on Mars. It covers three real places: Jezero Crater (Perseverance’s Cheyava Falls), Gale Crater (Curiosity’s Mount Sharp boxwork) and Deuteronilus Mensae, where a glacier lies buried under rock debris.

The user picks the stops. CAIRN runs A* over a 1-metre HiRISE elevation grid and finds the route that minimises walking energy (the Minetti model of walking on slopes) multiplied by fall risk. It avoids slopes above 25° and loose sand. One Dijkstra pass from the rover stores the fastest way home from every point. That makes an emergency re-route instant, and it powers the walk-back margin: the oxygen left if the crew turns back from the farthest point, keeping a 25% reserve.

Each plan gets six safety checks: terrain, oxygen, time, shelter within 30 minutes, radio and daylight. The Sun is placed for the real sol and time, and shadows are cast from the real terrain. A line-of-sight model shows where hills cut radio contact, and the crew can place relay masts that link to each other.

During a simulated EVA, CAIRN replays the real 20 May 2024 solar particle event measured by Curiosity’s RAD. When the dose rate passes three times the background, it reroutes the crew to the rover and reports the dose they avoided. The crew can also practise a suit leak or a twisted ankle.

Creativity: time as part of the simulation

Mission Control on Earth sees everything one light time late, 13 to 22 minutes for the EVA’s date, computed from JPL planet positions. It shows “Earth’s best guess” of where the crew is now, and its messages arrive late. After each walk, an autonomy debrief lists every decision the crew made alone, and when Earth could first have answered.

Free roam lets anyone walk the real terrain with Mars-gravity physics: 0.38 g traction, a bounding lope above 1.3 m/s, ballistic jumps, slides and falls. Oxygen, heart rate and breathing follow the effort. A second astronaut (EV2) can join from another device through crew sessions.

Benefits and impact

  • Mission planners can test routes and scenarios before an EVA.
  • Crews in training practise deciding under delay.
  • Students and the public can open it in a browser, on a phone, even offline, and understand what walking on Mars demands.

The pitch is simple: on Mars, help is always late, so the crew needs the answers before they leave the rover.

Tools and technologies

  • App: TypeScript, Three.js (WebGL 2), Vite and Web Workers, running in any modern browser.
  • Hab server: Node.js 24 with WebSockets. It relays data with the light-time delay and stores the field notebook.
  • Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj, shapely and Pillow.
  • Speech: on-device speech-to-text (Whisper via transformers.js) and a free neural voice (Kokoro) for directions.
  • Deployment: Railway.
  • Testing: 135 automated tests.

Data

The app uses 14 datasets from NASA, USGS and JPL:

  • HiRISE elevation and imagery
  • CRISM minerals
  • THEMIS thermal
  • the USGS geologic map
  • MEDA and REMS weather
  • RAD radiation
  • DONKI space weather
  • rover traverses and Navcam photos

What we considered

  • Data honesty: every number traces to a source listed in the app. Suit and body figures are labelled as demo assumptions, and the gap in the RAD storm record is a labelled model, scaled to NASA’s reported 8,100 µGy.
  • Access: a colour-blind-safe palette, keyboard and screen-reader support, phones and offline use.
  • Real places: sites chosen for real science, including water ice for future crews.
